newsitem.title: USA: Lincoln deal strengthens life business.
newsitem.headline: Lincoln deal strengthens life business.

text.p: Lincoln National Corp, a major force in the U.S. annuity market, will substantially strengthen its weaker life insurance operation with the acquisition of CIGNA Corp's individual life insurance business.
Meanwhile, CIGNA got a very attractive price to exit the non-core business as it increases its commitment to employee benefits and healthcare, analysts said.
The sale of the business also raised hopest CIGNA will also sell its property-casualty business, analysts said.

"It kind of signals in their corporate decision making process an interest in focusing on healthcare and employee benefit type transactions, which has got to raise the question is (property-casualty) a keeper," Sanford C. Bernstein analyst Weston Hicks said.
CIGNA shares rose 5-7/8, or about three percent, to close at 196-1/2.
And if CIGNA shares rallied so sharply on the sale of this business, "just think what it would do if they got out of the P-C business," Hicks said.

Lincoln National, for its part, flush with cash from the sale of its non-core property casualty business, strengthens the position of its life insurance operation, while reducing its dependence on its main annuity business, said Mark Puccia, director of Standard & Poor's insurance rating services.
Although Lincoln National was the twelfth largest life insurance company based on 1995 assets, life insurance has been a much smaller part of its overall financial service business.
Lincoln National "really wanted to diversify earnings and revenues," Puccia said.

Lincoln National, which expects to receive $2.15 billion agreed in after-tax proceeds from the sale of its American States Financial Corp property-casualty business, agreed on Monday to buy CIGNA's individual life business for $1.4 billion.
Although "Lincoln National paid a healthy price for this acquisition, they did at least invest in a line of business that makes a lot of sense for them," Puccia said.
Lincoln National's individual life business has been just a mediocre performer, Puccia said.
"So what they're doing is acquiring management talent from a very healthy block of business," Puccia said.
This deal "certainly raises their visibility in the world of invididual life," Puccia said.
Lincoln National chief executive Ian Rolland told Reuters in an interview he expects the CIGNA business to contribute $0.21 a share to Lincoln National earnings in 1998 and $0.22 a share in 1999.
Lincoln National, based in Fort Wayne, Ind., expects the deal to close by year-end.
Philadelphia-based CIGNA, which valued the deal at $1.6 billion, said it plans to use most of the proceeds from the sale of the business for share repurchase.

Internal growth and acquisitions are still high priorities for CIGNA, but the company said it does not have much appetite for another large deal at the moment, following its recent $1.7 billion acquisition of Healthsource Inc.
The deal will have little impact on CIGNA's earnings, Salomon analyst Michael Smith said. But, with this transaction "the company demonstrated that everything is for sale," he said.
